title: Area, diagonals and volume you will actually use
hook: Cable sizes are printed in mm², an area, not a width. If one solid round wire is twice as wide across as another, how many times as much cross-section does it have?
oneBreath: Area is how many unit squares cover a shape, so a rectangle is length × width, and a triangle is half the rectangle around it, using the height at right angles to its base. A circle's circumference is 2πr and its area is πr², both from the radius, so halve a diameter first; a solid round wire's cross-section is πr², and a ring is the big circle less the small one. Area units scale by the square: 1 cm² is a 10 by 10 grid of 1 mm squares, so 100 mm², not 10, which is also why doubling a side makes four times the area. In a right-angled triangle the squares on the two shorter sides add up to the square on the hypotenuse, the longest side, opposite the right angle, and a square root undoes the square. That gives a rectangle's diagonal, a straight run across a room, the distance between two grid points and even the diagonal through a box. A box or a cylinder holds its base area times its length, a litre is a 10 cm cube and a thousand of them fill a cubic metre, so a tank's size gives its litres, and with the liquid's density, its mass.

calibration.q: A floor is a rectangle 4 m long and 3 m wide. What is its area?
calibration.why: Area multiplies: 4 rows of 3 one-metre squares is 12 m². 14 m adds all four sides, which is the perimeter, and 7 adds just two sides.

calibration.q: A right-angled triangle has its two shorter sides 6 m and 8 m. How long is its longest side?
calibration.why: Square the shorter sides and add: 36 + 64 = 100, then the square root undoes the square, so 10 m. 14 m just adds the sides, and 100 m forgets the square root.
